summary: Paul, a prisoner, urges a life worthy of the call: one body and one Spirit, with varied gifts given to build up Christ’s body.

context.title: One body, many gifts
paragraphs: Chapter 4 opens the second, practical part of Ephesians: the “therefore” turns from what God has done to how believers should live. [c1] Paul writes as a prisoner, as he did at 3:1. [c2] The church he addressed was made up of Jews and Gentiles, so the call to keep unity answered a real danger of division. [c3]

Verses 4-6 name seven things that are one: body, Spirit, hope, Lord, faith, baptism, and God the Father of all. [c4] Ellicott calls these verses the final summary of the letter’s teaching on the unity of the Church. [c5] Verse 7 then turns to the other side of that unity, the diversity of gifts given to each believer. [c6]

The reading leaves out verses 8-10, where Paul quotes a psalm about gifts given from on high, and resumes with the gifts themselves. [c7] They are people: apostles, prophets, evangelists, and pastors who are also teachers. [c8] Later Christian usage gave the name evangelist to the writers of the four Gospels, Matthew among them. [c9]

translationNotes.summary: Greek says “the prisoner in the Lord”: the phrase ties Paul’s chains to his union with Christ.
translationNotes.body: Desmios means one who is bound, a captive or prisoner. [c10] Thayer reads the phrase in the same sense as “prisoner of Christ Jesus” in 3:1: the truth Paul preached has put him in bonds. [c11] The Cambridge Bible keeps the literal “in the Lord”, since his bonds are due to his union with Christ and so lend weight to his appeal. [c12]

translationNotes.summary: Paul’s image is walking: conduct that matches the calling, a phrase he uses in several letters.
translationNotes.body: The adverb axiōs means suitably or worthily, in a manner worthy of something. [c13] Paul pairs it with the verb walk again in Col 1:10 and 1 Thess 2:12, and walking is his usual picture for the whole conduct of life. [c14] The Cambridge Bible notes that no human walk is ideally worthy of the call, yet conduct can truly correspond to it when governed by divine motives. [c15]

translationNotes.summary: Commentators differ on whether this is a oneness of spirit among believers or the unity the Holy Spirit creates.
translationNotes.body: Barnes reads the phrase as oneness of spirit, a unity of affection, and not a direct reference to the Holy Spirit. [c16] The Cambridge Bible and Vincent instead take it as the unity which the Holy Spirit effects. [c17] On either reading the verb is to keep: the unity already exists and is to be guarded with eager diligence, which is the force of spoudazontes. [c18][c19]

translationNotes.summary: In the New Testament an evangelist is a preacher of the gospel, not yet the writer of a Gospel.
translationNotes.body: Thayer defines the word as a bringer of good tidings, used in the New Testament for heralds of salvation who were not apostles. [c20] It occurs only three times: here, of Philip in Acts 21:8, and in 2 Tim 4:5. [c21] The Cambridge Bible compares it with “missionary”: a function of proclaiming the gospel rather than a defined order in the Church. [c22]

original.gloss: for the fitting out of the saints

translationNotes.summary: Katartismos is a word for fitting out or setting right, used of ships, bones and mended nets.
translationNotes.body: The noun appears only here in the New Testament, and in classical Greek it was used of refitting a ship or setting a bone. [c23] The related verb describes James and John mending their nets in Mt 4:21. [c24] Readers divide on what follows: the Cambridge Bible has the saints equipped for their own work of service, while Barnes assigns the work of ministry to the appointed ministers. [c25]

claims.text: Ephesians 4:1 begins the second part of the epistle, moving from the spiritual aspects of redemption to their manifestation in conduct.
Paul calls himself a prisoner in Eph 4:1 and in Eph 3:1.
The Ephesian church was composed of Jews and Gentiles, and there was danger of division.
Eph 4:4-6 names one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism and one God and Father of all.
Ellicott regards Eph 4:1-6 as the final summary of the epistle’s doctrine of the unity of the Church.
Eph 4:7 presents the diversity of gifts as a motive to unity from the opposite side.
Eph 4:8, omitted in this reading, quotes a psalm about ascending on high and giving gifts.
Eph 4:11 lists apostles, prophets, evangelists, and pastors and teachers, the last two under one article and regarded as one ministry.
At a later time the name evangelist was given to the writers of the four Gospels: Matthew, Mark, Luke and John.
Δέσμιος means bound, a captive, a prisoner.
Thayer takes ὁ δέσμιος ἐν κυρίῳ in Eph 4:1 in the same sense as ὁ δέσμιος τοῦ Χριστοῦ Ἰησοῦ, one whom Christ’s truth that he preached has put in bonds.
The Cambridge Bible renders literally “the prisoner in the Lord”: his bonds are due to his union with Christ and are a strong argument with his converts.
Ἀξίως means suitably, worthily, in a manner worthy of.
Paul uses ἀξίως with the verb walk in Col 1:10 and 1 Thess 2:12, and walk denotes the moral conduct of life.
No human walk is ideally worthy of the calling, but it can be so practically when governed by divine motives.
Barnes takes the unity of the Spirit as oneness of spirit, a unity of affection, not a reference to the one Holy Spirit.
The Cambridge Bible and Vincent take the unity of the Spirit as the oneness effected by the Holy Spirit.
The oneness of the Spirit already exists and is to be kept (τηρεῖν), even when Christians are not careful of it.
Σπουδάζοντες originally means making haste, hence giving diligence, and is stronger than “endeavouring”.
Thayer defines εὐαγγελιστής as a bringer of good tidings, a name given in the NT to heralds of salvation who are not apostles.
Εὐαγγελιστής occurs three times in the NT: Eph 4:11, Acts 21:8 (of Philip) and 2 Tim 4:5.
Like “missionary”, evangelist indicates a special personal function of proclaiming the gospel rather than a defined ecclesiastical order.
Καταρτισμός occurs only in Eph 4:12 in the NT and was used in classical Greek of refitting a ship or setting a bone.
The kindred verb καταρτίζω is used of mending nets in Mt 4:21.
The Cambridge Bible reads Eph 4:12 as the equipment of the saints for their own work of service, while Barnes takes the work of the ministry as that of the officers listed.
